analysis.one_liner: Quadruples the federal tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4%
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the stock buyback excise tax from 1% to 4% never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would quadruple the federal excise tax on companies buying back their own stock, from 1% to 4%. It would also stop companies from shrinking the tax by subtracting shares they hand to their highest-paid executives. Revenue would flow to the Treasury; nothing in the bill earmarks it.
analysis.who_benefits: The U.S. Treasury and taxpayers generally, through the added revenue the higher tax would raise from companies that repurchase stock [S2][S3]. Workers could benefit if companies respond by shifting cash from buybacks toward wages or investment, though that behavior change is not guaranteed. The bill also removes a break that lets companies offset the tax with shares given to covered executives, closing a route around the tax for corporate leadership [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4%, collecting more revenue from companies that spend cash buying back their own shares [S2][S3].

Closes an offset: under current law a company's taxable buyback amount is reduced by the value of stock it issues; the bill would exclude stock issued to covered employees (the highly paid executives defined in tax code section 162(m)(3)) from that offset, so companies can no longer shrink the tax by granting executives shares [S3].
The higher rate would apply to repurchases made after enactment, so the change would take effect immediately rather than being phased in [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations that repurchase their own stock would pay four times the current excise tax, and their shareholders would bear the cost through lower share value or smaller distributions. Executives receiving company stock would lose the ability of their employers to use those grants to reduce the buyback tax [S3]. Because buybacks return cash to all shareholders, some of the burden falls indirectly on ordinary investors whose retirement funds hold index funds and other diversified stock portfolios.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies buying back stock and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every covered repurchase, so its burden lands on all shareholders of companies buying back stock, including ordinary retirement savers whose index funds and pension portfolios hold the same shares [S3].

The bill sets a rate change only; it does not direct the new revenue to any specific public purpose, so its benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on how Congress later spends the money [S2][S3].

Buybacks are one of several ways companies return cash to investors, and a higher tax could push some of that cash toward other shareholder payouts like dividends rather than toward wages or investment, limiting any benefit to workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, targeted tool: it makes buybacks modestly more expensive and closes a specific executive-stock loophole, while leaving companies free to keep repurchasing stock. Its cost is real but diffuse — spread across shareholders, including retirement savers — and its benefit is real but indirect, arriving only as general federal revenue rather than as any direct gain for workers. It would have been a modest corrective, not a transformation, and the fact that it never even reached a committee vote means neither the benefits nor the costs were ever tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a markup or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on February 14, 2023, joined by Senators Wyden, Schatz, Van Hollen, Reed, Lujan, and Baldwin [S3][S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
Cosponsorship grew to 9 senators, all Democrats [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote was reported in the record, and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5][S1].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill; any revival would have required starting over in a new Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that spend heavily on stock buybacks — and the executives whose stock grants could reduce the buyback tax — kept the lower 1% rate and the existing offset, with no new cost to their shareholders.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies doing buybacks and their executives

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to measure, but every one of the bill's 10 supporters was a Democrat and no Republican signed on, so the bill lived entirely on one side of the aisle before dying quietly [S4].

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations that repurchase stock
industries.note: The bill would quadruple their buyback tax from 1% to 4% and remove the executive-stock offset, making repurchases meaningfully more expensive. These companies' interest in keeping buybacks cheap runs against the revenue and market-discipline goals of the tax [S3].

Covered executives (the highest-paid defined under tax code section 162(m)(3)) would lose the arrangement under which shares issued to them reduce their company's taxable buyback amount. Their compensation is often tied to buyback-boosted share prices [S3].

Shareholders absorb the higher excise tax through reduced returns on companies that buy back stock; pension funds and index-fund savers hold those shares too, though they also have a stake in Treasury revenue.
